z-m-30-01.title: What comes after 1, 2, 4?
z-m-30-01.topic: Powers of a matrix: how many values does it take to settle a pattern?
z-m-30-01.goal: Realize that in powers of a matrix, several rules can fit a small number of values, filter out candidate rules and revise your judgment as you go, and explain that you can be sure of a general formula only after finding the reason (the structure).
z-m-30-01.material: B is a 2×2 matrix, and its four entries (row 1 column 1, row 1 column 2, row 2 column 1, row 2 column 2) are all 1. B^n is the matrix you get by multiplying B n times. All entries are real numbers and n is an integer that is 1 or more. Two friends are talking about the entries of B³. One says, "The entries of B¹ and B² are 1 and 2, so B³ is 3," and the other says, "I'm not sure yet. Let's multiply more." Each time data is revealed, revise your judgment or hold to it.
z-m-30-01.thinking.0: When generalizing a rule from little data, also considering the other rules that are possible
z-m-30-01.thinking.1: Adjusting your judgment and degree of confidence according to new information
z-m-30-01.thinking.2: Finding the first line that goes wrong in a solution and explaining the cause
z-m-30-01.thinking.3: Making a general formula using letters (p, n) and writing the reason
z-m-30-01.prereq.0: Multiplication of 2×2 matrices (one entry of the product = the sum of products of the entries of one row of the front matrix and one column of the back matrix) and powers A^n = A multiplied n times
z-m-30-01.prereq.1: Reading expressions that contain the letters n and p and finding simple number patterns
z-m-30-01.prereq.2: School-order assumption: the H2 of this task is only a difficulty label in production and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. We assume it comes right after matrix multiplication is learned, and induction or determinants are not needed.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one step at a time. At every step, choose your present judgment about what the entries of the powers of B will be.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write every rule that fits the numbers so far, and compare which of them the new information eliminates.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether you chose by thinking of only one rule, or whether you also considered other rules.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.info: B¹ is B itself, so all four entries are 1. When B² was multiplied out directly, all four entries were 2.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: What about the entries of B³? Choose your present judgment.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.after: The two pieces of data explain both 3 and 4. You can take one rule as a 'working hypothesis,' but before checking it is reasonable to keep your judgment open.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: All entries are 3. After 1, 2, the rule of increasing by 1 continues
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: There are rules that fit 1, 2 other than 'increase by 1.' With only two data points, it is too early to settle on one rule.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: All entries are 4. After 1, 2, the rule of doubling continues
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The doubling rule also fits 1, 2, but so does 'increase by 1.' Notice that it is too early to choose just one and be sure.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We can't decide between 3 and 4 right now, so check by multiplying out B³ directly
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You recognized that the two data points fit several rules and put off your judgment. You even thought of the action to check (multiplying directly).
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: All entries are 2. It is a matrix with all entries the same, so the value does not change anymore
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: In B², the value already changed from 1 to 2. That the entries are the same does not mean the value does not change.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.info: When B³ was multiplied out directly, all four entries were 4. So far it is 1, 2, 4. The rule that fits these numbers is not only 'doubling.' Adding the previous two values and then adding 1 gives 1, 2, 4, 7, ..., and this fits too.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you judge now about B⁴?
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.after: Thanks to B³, 'increase by 1' has been eliminated. But the doubling rule and the 1, 2, 4, 7 rule cannot be told apart until B⁴ is calculated. You need to gather more data or find the reason why.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Settle on the doubling rule and write that all entries of B⁴ are 8
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It is true that the three values fit doubling, but the 1, 2, 4, 7 rule fits too. You have not yet separated the two.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Regard the 4 of B³ as a calculation mistake and keep the first rule that all are 3
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: If you blame the directly calculated value on a mistake, you can keep your first judgment but have no basis. Re-checking the calculation is different from throwing it away.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: There are several rules, so make no guess at all from this data
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: 'Increase by 1' no longer fits. That the remaining rules have been reduced in number is also information.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Drop 'increase by 1,' and sort out the remaining two rules with B⁴
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You dropped the rule that does not fit the data and even thought of a way to separate the remaining rules.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.info: I looked for a reason. Say all four entries of B^n are the same number k. One entry of B^(n+1) = B^n × B is (k × 1) + (k × 1) = 2k. It is the same calculation for all four entries. All the entries of B¹ are 1.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now how do you judge the entries of B^n and B⁵?
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.after: The shape in which all entries are the same is kept every time and the value doubles, so the entries of B^n are 2^(n−1). The judgment that was left open at first as 'whether it is 3 or 4' narrowed in the order of data → candidate rules → reason. A student who calculated B⁴ directly reaches the same conclusion.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The entries of B^n are all n, and those of B⁵ are all 5
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The n rule already went off at B³. It also does not fit the new information (2k each time we multiply).
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The entries of B^n are all 2^(n−1), and those of B⁵ are all 16
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You connected it all the way to the reason 'each multiplication gives 2k' applying to every n.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is likely to be 2^(n−1), but I won't be sure before multiplying out B⁵ directly
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The attitude of wanting to check is good. But the new information is a reason that holds for any n. Think about how that reason affects your confidence.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: B⁴ is 7, so B⁵ is all 12
z-m-30-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You kept the 1, 2, 4, 7 rule. Check whether it fits the new information that k becomes 2k.
z-m-30-01.s.s1.reflect: From putting off your judgment at first to becoming confident at the end, what changed your confidence? What difference did gathering three more data points and finding the 'reason' make to your confidence?
z-m-30-01.s.s2.prompt: Hayun, a classmate, found the entries of the powers of C = 3B (a matrix whose four entries are all 3) as below. Choose the first line that goes wrong.
z-m-30-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one of the entries of C and calculate directly the (row 1, column 1) entry of C multiplied by itself twice.
z-m-30-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the directly calculated value with the value on each line and find the first line where they differ.
z-m-30-01.s.s2.line.1: All entries of B² are 2, so all entries of C² are 3 × 2 = 6.
z-m-30-01.s.s2.line.2: In the same way C³ = 3B³, and all entries of B³ are 4, so all entries of C³ are 3 × 4 = 12.
z-m-30-01.s.s2.line.3: So the entries of C^n are 3 × 2^(n−1).
z-m-30-01.s.s2.explain: In line 1, the constant 3 is present once in each of the two factors, but it was taken out only once. In (3B)(3B) the 3 appears twice, so C² = 9B², and all entries are 9 × 2 = 18. If you square C directly and calculate just one entry, 3×3 + 3×3 = 18, so you can confirm it differs from 6. Lines 2 to 4 inherited the expression of line 1 and are wrong. Line 3 too, for the same reason: C³ = 27B³ and the entries are 108.
z-m-30-01.s.s3.prompt: This time, consider a matrix P whose four entries are all p (p is a positive integer). Express the entries of P^n, P multiplied n times, in terms of p and n, and write why you can say so.
z-m-30-01.s.s3.hint.0: For p=1 and p=2, multiply out P² directly and compare the entries.
z-m-30-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write as an expression how the entries of P² are connected to the entries of P and p, and check whether the same thing happens in P³.
z-m-30-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The entries of P^n are ... Because ...
z-m-30-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the entry 2^(n−1) of B^n come out again in my expression when p=1?
z-m-30-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I check that it matches the values multiplied directly by putting in n=1 and n=2?
z-m-30-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I write the skeleton of the reason, such as 'why calculating one entry is enough' or 'by factoring out B'?
z-m-30-01.s.s3.model.0: The entries of P^n are all p^n × 2^(n−1). If we write P = pB, then P^n = p^n B^n, and the entries of B^n double each time.
z-m-30-01.s.s3.modelNote.0: The method of factoring out B
z-m-30-01.s.s3.model.1: As p, 2p², 4p³, ..., the entries become 2p times as large each time we multiply once. The four entries keep the same shape and one entry is p×k + p×k = 2pk, so the entries of P^n are p × (2p)^(n−1).
z-m-30-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: The method that starts from the change of one multiplication. The expression is the same as the previous answer.
